sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Constitutional Mandate**: Governed by **Part XII** of the Constitution of India (Articles 268-293), outlining the division of taxing powers and revenue sharing.
• **Vertical Devolution**: The sharing of total divisible pool of tax revenues between the **Central Government** and the **State Governments** collectively, determined by successive Finance Commissions.
• **Horizontal Devolution**: The distribution of the states' share of tax revenues **among individual states** based on equity, need, performance, and demographic criteria.
• **Divisible Pool**: Comprises all taxes levied and collected by the Union Government, **excluding** specific cesses and surcharges levied for specific purposes (which are non-shareable) and Union Territories' tax revenues.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Taxes Levied & Collected by Centre, Assigned to States (Art 269)
Taxes on interstate trade or commerce (e.g., Central Sales Tax historically).
Collected by Centre but entirely assigned to the states where they originate.
Rarely tested independently post-GST, but important for constitutional scope.
Levied & Collected by Centre but Distributed between Centre & States (Art 270)
All taxes and duties referred to in the Union List except cesses, surcharges, and specific fees.
Shared as per the vertical devolution formula recommended by the Finance Commission.
Core concept for Prelims and GS-2 questions on fiscal federalism.
Levied by Parliament for specific public purposes (e.g., Health and Education Cess, Infrastructure Cesses).
Retained entirely by the Central Government; **not part of the divisible pool**.
High-yield Prelims trap regarding recent trends of rising cess collection.

items.definition: A quasi-judicial constitutional body constituted every 5 years by the President to recommend the principles governing the vertical and horizontal distribution of tax revenues.

The structural mismatch where the Centre collects a majority of tax revenues due to economies of scale and administrative efficiency, while States bear heavy expenditure responsibilities for social and economic development.
Disparities in revenue-raising capacities and costs of providing public services among different states due to varying levels of economic development, geography, and population.
A cess levied under the GST (Compensation to States) Act, 2017 to bridge revenue shortfalls of states during the transition phase of GST implementation.

items.title: Major Geographical & Economic Distribution Dynamics
items.content:
• **Source vs. Residence Principle**: Income tax and corporate tax collections skew heavily toward financial and industrial hubs (e.g., Maharashtra, Karnataka, Delhi, Tamil Nadu).
• **Correction Mechanism**: Horizontal devolution heavily weights income distance, population, and area to transfer resources from surplus/industrial states to resource-deficient and populous states (e.g., Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Madhya Pradesh).

items.title: Challenges, Reforms & Forward Strategy
items.content:
• **Cessification Trend**: Increasing reliance by the Centre on cesses and surcharges reduces the size of the divisible pool, drawing criticism from fiscal federalism advocates.
• **Performance vs. Need Trade-off**: Balancing redistributive justice (supporting poorer states) with incentive-compatible criteria (rewarding tax effort and demographic performance).

items.title: Mnemonic for 15th Finance Commission Horizontal Devolution Criteria
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym / Phrase**: 'I P A F D' (Imagine Poor Andhra Falling Down)
• **Decoded Meaning**: 
  1. **I**ncome Distance (45%)
  2. **P**opulation 2011 (15%)
  3. **A**rea (15%)
  4. **F**orest & Ecology (10%)
  5. **D**emographic Performance (12.5%) + Tax Effort (2.5%)
• **Prelims Exam Value**: Instantly verifies weightage percentages in matching-list or statement-based MCQs.

items.title: Retention Rule of Thumb
items.content: • **Core Formula / Rule**: Remember that 'Cesses and Surcharges' never enter the divisible tax pool unless explicitly specified by statute, protecting Central revenue mobilization during emergencies.

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC frequently states that 'all taxes collected by the Union government are shared with the states.' This is false because cesses, surcharges, and specific duties levied under Article 271 are excluded from the divisible pool.

Mains Value Addition: In GS-2 answers regarding fiscal federalism, quote the 15th Finance Commission's innovation of rewarding 'Demographic Performance' to incentivize states that successfully managed population growth.

keyTakeaways: Tax revenue distribution is regulated by Part XII of the Constitution and operationalized through the Finance Commission under Article 280.
Vertical devolution addresses structural fiscal mismatch between Centre and States, while horizontal devolution corrects inter-state economic disparities.
The proliferation of non-shareable cesses and surcharges remains a key friction point in contemporary Indian fiscal federalism.
